questions.question: [Consumer Rights] Q: What are the three statutory rights when buying goods?
questions.correctAnswer: Goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and match their description. These are implied terms under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 — if any is breached, the consumer has a right to a remedy.
questions.explanation: Goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and match their description. These are implied terms under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 — if any is breached, the consumer has a right to a remedy.

questions.question: [Consumer Rights] Q: What remedies are available for faulty goods under the Consumer Rights Act 2015?
questions.correctAnswer: Within 30 days: full refund (short-term right to reject). After 30 days but within 6 months: repair or replacement. If repair or replacement fails: refund (may be reduced for use). After 6 months: consumer must prove the fault was present at delivery.
questions.explanation: Within 30 days: full refund (short-term right to reject). After 30 days but within 6 months: repair or replacement. If repair or replacement fails: refund (may be reduced for use). After 6 months: consumer must prove the fault was present at delivery.

questions.question: [Consumer Rights] Q: What rights do consumers have when services are poor?
questions.correctAnswer: Services must be performed with reasonable care and skill, within a reasonable time and at a reasonable price. If not, the consumer can require the trader to redo the service or, if that is impossible, claim a price reduction.
questions.explanation: Services must be performed with reasonable care and skill, within a reasonable time and at a reasonable price. If not, the consumer can require the trader to redo the service or, if that is impossible, claim a price reduction.

questions.question: [Contract Law] Q: What three elements must exist for a valid contract?
questions.correctAnswer: Offer and acceptance (agreement), consideration (something of value exchanged), and intention to create legal relations (the parties intend the agreement to be legally binding).
questions.explanation: Offer and acceptance (agreement), consideration (something of value exchanged), and intention to create legal relations (the parties intend the agreement to be legally binding).

questions.question: [Contract Law] Q: What is the difference between an offer and an invitation to treat?
questions.correctAnswer: An offer is a definite statement of willingness to be bound; an invitation to treat is merely an invitation for others to make offers (e.g. goods on a shelf, advertisements). Only an offer can be accepted to form a contract.
questions.explanation: An offer is a definite statement of willingness to be bound; an invitation to treat is merely an invitation for others to make offers (e.g. goods on a shelf, advertisements). Only an offer can be accepted to form a contract.

questions.question: [Contract Law] Q: What is consideration and why is it needed?
questions.correctAnswer: Consideration is something of value exchanged between the parties — each must give and receive something. It is needed because a promise without consideration is generally not legally binding (a bare promise is only enforceable as a deed).
questions.explanation: Consideration is something of value exchanged between the parties — each must give and receive something. It is needed because a promise without consideration is generally not legally binding (a bare promise is only enforceable as a deed).

questions.question: [Courts & Court Structure] Q: What is the difference between criminal and civil courts?
questions.correctAnswer: Criminal courts deal with offences against the state (prosecuted by the Crown); civil courts deal with disputes between individuals or organisations, where the claimant sues the defendant.
questions.explanation: Criminal courts deal with offences against the state (prosecuted by the Crown); civil courts deal with disputes between individuals or organisations, where the claimant sues the defendant.

questions.question: [Courts & Court Structure] Q: What cases does the Crown Court hear?
questions.correctAnswer: Indictable offences (serious crimes like murder and rape), either-way offences sent from the Magistrates' Court, and appeals from the Magistrates' Court against conviction or sentence.
questions.explanation: Indictable offences (serious crimes like murder and rape), either-way offences sent from the Magistrates' Court, and appeals from the Magistrates' Court against conviction or sentence.

questions.question: [Courts & Court Structure] Q: What are the three divisions of the High Court?
questions.correctAnswer: Queen's Bench (contract and tort), Chancery (business, trusts, tax) and Family (divorce, children, financial remedies).
questions.explanation: Queen's Bench (contract and tort), Chancery (business, trusts, tax) and Family (divorce, children, financial remedies).
